source: R 4.4.0 stats::glm(family = binomial) Monte Carlo, evaluated independently of SciPy and of the PowerBench simulator
purpose: Adjudicates the Demidenko (2007) Wald reference for a balanced binary predictor. Guards against regression to the pre-2026-08-03 implementation, which evaluated the binomial variance only at the baseline probability and produced sign-varying error in required N (+6% to +21% for p0 < 0.5, but -6% at p0 = 0.5).

design.test: Wald z on the logistic slope from stats::glm

cases.label: sample size produced by the Demidenko binary-predictor reference
cases.note: PowerBench reference gives 0.8002 at this N. Agreement within Monte Carlo error.

cases.label: sample size from pwrss under its default NORMAL predictor - a different estimand
cases.note: Recorded deliberately as an assumption-difference case study, not a tool disagreement. pwrss.z.logreg(method = 'demidenko') defaults to 'Predictor Dist.: Normal' and returns N = 249; under a balanced BINARY predictor that sample size delivers 0.31 power. A cross-tool comparison that ignored the predictor distribution would wrongly read this as a 3.4x defect in one of the two tools.

external_tool_comparison.call: pwrss.z.logreg(p0 = 0.30, odds.ratio = 1.5, power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05, alternative = 'not equal', method = 'demidenko')
external_tool_comparison.explanation: pwrss defaults to a standard-normal predictor, where the effect is a one-SD change; PowerBench's binary branch defines the effect as the contrast between two equally sized groups. Both are correct for their own estimand. Monte Carlo with a balanced binary predictor confirms PowerBench's N; pwrss must be called with dist = list(dist = 'bernoulli', prob = 0.5) to be comparable.
